en.html:
The Dragoon holds its sword in the high right stance, the orthodox warrior's form. Facing it, the old man takes his short sword at middle guard, ready to meet the heavy blade.

A short sword starts from receiving and goes on to attack. That is its basic axis, and with its shorter reach it cannot be otherwise.

But the old man is deliberately breaking this rule. His point hangs a little low, his weight leans too far forward. For receiving, very inconvenient.

His intention is plain: not to receive, but to attack.

Against a long sword that rules the range, this is reckless, even madness, I would say. A master of the short sword may steal the long sword's distance and take control of it, but only with feints and bargaining. To attack openly is out of the question.

What hidden plan does the old man carry into such violence?

—None.

This is not the state of emptiness. It is the state of foolishness.

Then only one road is left. He too has to become a fool and face it.

Loud, certainly. But only a sound. Down on the ground it may have shaken things considerably; up here, only our eardrums were shaken.

Immediately afterward, Gassan became visible. And the man himself did not notice at once.

...That does not fit. Suppose the roar startled him into dropping the art—a Fuma chief, startled by a noise? Even so, if he had dropped it himself, how could he fail to notice? And if he was not startled, why should the art break at all?

The two sides will not add up. This contradiction, here. Behind it is the truth.

But what truth!? One more thing—one foothold for the thought—

...Caught! Beside an old shrine, two armored warriors—<ruby>Mount Haguro and Mount Yudono<rt>・・・・・・・</rt></ruby>!

These two were the real identity of the Kirigakure art. Hidden on the ground, they were the casters <ruby>putting the art on Gassan<rt>・・・・・・・・・・・</rt></ruby>!

Now the whole thing fitted. Such an unreasonable art, and no wonder: two frames were supplying their combined strength. Probably one was doing the optics and the other the signals. And Gassan's strange chanting was not the <ruby>incantation<rt>command</rt></ruby> of the art; it was a signal to those two!

Those two do nothing but maintain the art; Gassan does nothing but fight. With that arrangement, what mystery is left in its lasting so unnaturally long?

One invincible warrior we had been facing—made from three frames. Just as the Three Mountains of Dewa make one faith!

The shock, presumably from the clash between the magistrate and Elder Yagenta, upset the casters' concentration and broke Kirigakure: a chance arrangement of fate. If that had not happened—we probably could not have broken this trinity.
